sections.heading: What is the Knapsack Pattern?
sections.content: The knapsack pattern is a family of DP problems where you choose items, each with a cost (weight) and a benefit (value), while staying within a limit (capacity, budget, target sum). In the 0/1 knapsack each item can be used at most once. In the unbounded knapsack an item can be used any number of times. The DP state is dp[w] (or dp[i][w]): the best value, the number of ways, or a yes/no answer for capacity w. Time is O(n * W), where n is the number of items and W is the capacity, which is called pseudo-polynomial because it depends on the numeric value of W.

Keywords: capacity, budget, subset sum, partition, target, each item once, unlimited supply, number of ways

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: You are packing a bag with a weight limit. For each item you ask one question: take it or leave it? Leaving it keeps the best value you already had for that capacity. Taking it gives the item's value plus the best you could do with the capacity that remains. dp[w] always stores the best answer for a bag of size w, and you improve it item by item. The only difference between 0/1 and unbounded is whether you are allowed to reuse the same item after taking it.

sections.heading: Why the Loop Direction Matters
sections.content: In a 1D array, dp[w - wt] must hold the value from BEFORE the current item was considered when you want to use each item once. Looping capacity downward guarantees that: the smaller index has not been updated yet for this item. Looping upward does the opposite: dp[w - wt] was already updated with the current item, so the item can be taken again and again. That is exactly the difference between 0/1 and unbounded.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Looping capacity upward in a 0/1 problem, which silently reuses items
Looping capacity downward in an unbounded problem, which stops reuse and gives wrong answers
Forgetting dp[0] = 1 (counting) or dp[0] = true (boolean) as the base case
Using Int.MAX_VALUE as infinity and adding 1 to it, which overflows
Swapping the loops in counting problems and counting permutations instead of combinations
Allocating a table of size total when the target is only total / 2
Not checking whether total is odd before halving in the partition problems
Applying greedy by value-per-weight to the 0/1 knapsack (it is only correct for the fractional version)
Calling O(n * W) polynomial: it is pseudo-polynomial, so a huge capacity needs another approach

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Knapsack problems pick items under a limit, and dp[w] stores the best answer for limit w
0/1 knapsack loops capacity downward, and unbounded knapsack loops capacity upward
Many problems are disguised: partition becomes subset sum, and target sum becomes counting subsets
Decide what dp stores: a boolean, a count, a minimum or a maximum, and initialize dp[0] accordingly
In counting problems, items outer gives combinations and the limit outer gives permutations
The running time O(n * W) is pseudo-polynomial, so it depends on the size of the capacity
